meanings.note: Used for time or order.

examples.trans: The next station is Seoul Station.

meanings.note: Action of coming together with someone.
Used mostly in negative sentences.
Refers to keeping in touch or receiving news.

없다.gloss: to not exist, to not have

meanings.en: to not exist, to not have
meanings.note: Opposite of 있다.
Adds plurality to 'all'.
Direction of movement toward the speaker.
A highly respectful title for teachers, doctors, or senior professionals.
Refers to the location close to the speaker.
Action of taking a seat.

안녕하다.gloss: to be well, to be at peace

meanings.en: to be well, to be at peace
meanings.note: Mainly used in greetings like '안녕하세요'.
Determiner form of 하나, used before a noun counter.
Counter for drinks in cups or glasses.

examples.trans: Please give me one cup of coffee.
I drank two glasses of water.

meanings.note: Can refer to objects, phone calls, or treatments.

examples.trans: He is not answering the phone.

meanings.note: Used with close friends or subordinates. Becomes 내 before the subject marker -ga.
Points to something close to the speaker.
Short for '프로그램' (program).
Loanword for Producer/Director in broadcasting.

examples.trans: I will become a famous PD.

meanings.note: Usually followed by -e to mean 'because of'.

examples.trans: I was late because of the rain.

meanings.note: The most common verb, often combined with nouns to create action verbs.
Often shortened to 거 in spoken Korean.
A polite, enthusiastic expression of agreement.
Refers to having knowledge or awareness.
English loanword.
Takes an object marker for the thing being liked.
Compound of lunch and time.

meanings.en: to become, to function, to be done
meanings.note: A highly versatile verb.

examples.trans: I want to become a doctor.

meanings.note: Can modify nouns or verbs.

meanings.en: to be sold out, to run out of stock
meanings.note: Sino-Korean term used in stores and commerce.
Can refer to a residence or casually to a restaurant/store.

그동안.gloss: during that time, up to now

meanings.en: during that time, up to now
meanings.note: Used to reflect on a past period.

examples.trans: Thank you for everything up to now.
Have you been well during that time?

meanings.note: Used to emphasize an adjective or verb.
Often used in fixed greetings to acknowledge someone's effort.

examples.trans: Thank you for your hard work.
You're going through a lot of trouble.

많다.gloss: to be many, to be much

meanings.en: to be many, to be much, to be abundant
meanings.note: Opposite of 적다.
Used to ask the reason.

이러다.gloss: to do this, to act like this

meanings.en: to do this, to act like this
meanings.note: Contracted from 이러하다.

examples.trans: Why are you acting like this?

meanings.note: Used before adjectives or verbs.

examples.trans: Please give me a little more.

meanings.note: Used in negative sentences to mean 'not anymore' or 'no longer'.
Placed directly before the verb or adjective.

보다.gloss: to see, to watch, to read

meanings.en: to see, to watch, to look at
meanings.note: Can also mean to take an exam or meet someone.
General word for human beings.
Opposite of 이다, typically used with the subject marker.
Indicates a high frequency of an action.
Humble equivalent of 보다 or 만나다, used toward elders.

examples.trans: How do you do? (I see you for the first time.)

meanings.note: Used to describe doing something with great effort.
Compound of 하다 (to do) and 주다 (to give).

examples.trans: Please help me (do helping for me).

meanings.note: Sino-Korean term, often used as a formal greeting.
Can refer to physical space or time ahead.

examples.trans: I look forward to your kind cooperation in the future.

meanings.note: Often used with 하다.
Used to form negative commands (e.g. -지 마세요).
